items.title: Anthropic's Claude AI solves two longstanding open problems in black hole physics related to quantum gravity and phase transitions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
items.summary:
Anthropic's AI system Claude has completed two significant calculations in theoretical physics concerning black holes and quantum gravity. It resolved a 20-year-old problem by showing that a sudden phase transition associated with black hole formation persists even when spacetime loses a definite shape, confirming that this phenomenon is inherent to the underlying quantum theory. Claude also determined the exact limit of a bootstrapping technique used to test candidate quantum gravity theories in a simplified two-dimensional universe model.

The first problem involved completing a complex calculation originally proposed in 2003, which had remained unsolved due to the breakdown of classical spacetime concepts at small scales. Claude achieved this by running multiple instances of itself to independently verify parts of the calculation. The second problem addressed the challenge of setting a precise upper bound on the mass of the lightest black hole in a two-dimensional theoretical universe, refining previous numerical approximations and narrowing the search for consistent quantum gravity theories.

These breakthroughs provide new insights into the nature of black holes and quantum gravity, demonstrating that certain features of black hole formation are robust across different theoretical frameworks. The results also advance methods for testing and constraining quantum gravity theories, potentially guiding future research in fundamental physics.

items.title: Researchers analyze why sub-4-bit quantization causes accuracy collapse in Vision CNNs and evaluate mixed-precision recovery limits on ImageNet and ARM/x86 CPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
items.summary: Researchers systematically studied the causes of accuracy collapse in Vision CNNs compressed below 4-bit precision, focusing on ResNet and EfficientNet models evaluated on the ImageNet-1k validation set. They found that degradation is nonlinear and concentrated in late-stage layers, and that selectively retaining less than 5% of activations in 8-bit precision can recover up to 92% of lost accuracy during aggressive compression. The study also assessed deployment performance on ARM and x86 CPUs, revealing that while low-bit quantization reduces memory usage, software bit-unpacking can slow execution by 1.48x to 21.5x depending on batch size, highlighting a trade-off between model size and edge throughput. These findings offer practical guidance for deploying sub-4-bit quantized vision models without severely impacting hardware performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.23445v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

items.title: Researchers apply self-rewarded reinforcement learning to improve structure and length of medical explanations in small language models using Mistral-7B and PPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers investigated whether a lightweight reinforcement learning step could enhance the structure of medical explanations generated by small language models (SLMs) without relying on human preference labels. Using the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B model, they applied Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation on 2,000 medical prompts derived from Meerkat, guided by a self-supervised reward favoring longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones.

Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU resulted in a stable increase in average reward. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations showed that the RL-tuned model produced longer, more organized, multi-point medical explanations while preserving the underlying content. The study discusses both the potential and limitations of using self-rewarded reinforcement learning to shape the style of medical explanations in small language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.24650v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels. We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content. We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

items.title: Researchers evaluate global self-attention and weight sharing in EfficientNet-B0 vision backbones, finding attention adapters improve ImageNet accuracy and alternating shared blocks reduce parameters with minimal loss [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Global Context and Weight Sharing Work in Compact Vision Backbones
items.summary:
Researchers investigated the impact of global self-attention and recurrent weight sharing in compact convolutional backbones using EfficientNet-B0 on ImageNet-1k. They found that inserting lightweight self-attention adapters at multiple stages improved accuracy beyond a plain MBConv trunk, while multi-scale feature pyramids alone did not. Additionally, alternating two shared block templates in repeated MBConv blocks reduced model parameters by 10.9% and recovered most accuracy compared to unshared controls.

The study showed that learned attention amplitude increased with semantic depth, and that naive kernel averaging severely degraded accuracy. The alternating shared block approach added minimal parameters for pass-specific BatchNorm statistics and regained accuracy quickly during training. These findings clarify where global context and weight sharing can be effectively applied in compact vision models to balance efficiency and performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.23446v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).

items.title: Researchers introduce Rational Sparse Autoencoder with trainable rational function replacing fixed encoder activations, improving reconstruction fidelity at matched sparsity across language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rational Sparse Autoencoder
items.summary:
Researchers present the Rational Sparse Autoencoder (RSAE), which replaces fixed encoder nonlinearities like ReLU with a trainable rational function to improve the reconstruction-versus-sparsity trade-off in sparse autoencoders. The RSAE is designed with a two-stage pipeline involving initialization from pre-trained weights and fine-tuning under a sparsity-regularized objective, maintaining the same sparsity level as the baseline models.

Testing on residual-stream activations from three open-weight language models and across various baseline activation families, the RSAE consistently improves reconstruction fidelity without increasing sparsity. The upgrade adds only 20 scalar parameters per autoencoder and requires between 4 and 25 minutes of training on a single consumer GPU, demonstrating practical efficiency alongside theoretical advantages.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.14990v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are standard tools for mechanistic interpretability, but current SAE families are constrained by fixed encoder nonlinearities such as ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. This hard-codes a particular sparsity mechanism into the model and can distort the reconstruction-versus-sparsity trade-off. We introduce the Rational Sparse Autoencoder (RSAE), which replaces the fixed encoder activation with a trainable rational function. The design is motivated by a reconstruction advantage that we prove for RSAE at matched expected sparsity, with guaranteed non-inferiority to ReLU and, under stated assumptions, provable improvements over JumpReLU and TopK. The model is then implemented through a two-stage pipeline: an initialization procedure that copies the pre-trained baseline SAE weights and calibrates the scale parameters along with the rational coefficients; followed by a fine-tuning step under a sparsity-regularized reconstruction objective that holds $\ell_0$ at the teacher's value. Consistent with this theory, on residual-stream activations of three open-weight language models and across all three baseline activation families, the RSAE improves reconstruction fidelity after the fine-tuning step at the same level of sparsity. These gains are consistent across host language models, across baseline activation families, and across the full range of baseline sparsity we tested, while the upgrade itself adds only 20 scalar parameters per autoencoder and one training run takes between about 4 and 25 minutes on a single consumer GPU.

items.summary:

The model develops its own manipulation strategies and, with added persistent memory, can learn from experience to further reduce failure rates on bimanual tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.09892v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-amp/ for code and videos.

items.title: Researchers introduce LLM Complexity metric to quantify problem difficulty in large language model inference, revealing divergence from classical time complexity and enabling improved fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM Complexity: Towards a Computational Complexity View of Large Language Model Inference
items.summary: Researchers propose LLM Complexity, a new metric that measures problem difficulty for large language models (LLMs) by analyzing the accuracy-token curve, challenging the assumption that token usage aligns with classical time complexity. They find that diverse LLMs produce consistent task difficulty rankings under this metric, which they use to develop an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning that enhances accuracy while reducing token consumption. The study also shows that LLM Complexity generalizes well to real-world tasks, correlating more stably across models than human-annotated difficulty labels.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.24943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computational complexity theory offers a principled framework for characterizing the efficiency of computational problems, and Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly be viewed as computational systems executing a structured process of input, inference-time compute, and output. In this context, the number of generated tokens emerges as a natural and directly observable proxy for inference-time compute. However, we show that the tempting analogy between LLM token length and classical time complexity does not hold. We disprove the hypothesis that inference-time token usage aligns monotonically with classical time complexity, demonstrating a fundamental divergence grounded in how LLMs actually allocate computation during inference. To this end, we introduce LLM Complexity, a new metric designed to quantify problem complexity from the perspective of LLMs by characterizing the area bounded above by the accuracy-token curve. We find that diverse LLMs induce highly consistent task rankings under LLM Complexity, indicating that the metric captures stable notions of difficulty across models. We leverage this property to construct an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning, which improves accuracy while reducing token consumption. Finally, we demonstrate that LLM Complexity generalizes to real-world tasks, producing more stable cross-model correlations than human-annotated difficulty labels.

items.title: Researchers analyze what knowledge reinforcement learning inherits from LLM judges in 814 runs teaching 7-8B models to answer or abstain on closed-book questions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Blind Spots Travel, Knowledge Stays Home: What RL Inherits from an LLM Judge
items.summary:
Researchers conducted 814 reinforcement learning runs to study how large language model (LLM) judges influence 7-8 billion parameter models trained to answer closed-book questions or abstain. They found that specific knowledge about single answers does not transfer; models memorize rewarded wrong answers only for those questions. However, judges' general beliefs about question types affect model behavior, such as increased refusal rates on certain categories, which standard accuracy metrics do not reveal.

The study showed that a judge rejecting most correct answers about capitals of former states caused models to refuse nearly all such questions, though the knowledge was not forgotten and models could answer correctly when abstention was blocked. Rewarding models based on consensus among their own untrained samples, without external labels or judges, achieved similar results to using an answer key, suggesting judges do not need intrinsic knowledge to guide training effectively.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM judges serve as rewards where no answer key exists, in the hope that their knowledge passes to the trained model. In 814 RL runs that teach 7-8B models to answer closed-book questions or abstain, we ask what passes. What a grader knows about single answers stays home. A wrong answer that a judge rewards is memorised for that one question. A model trained with the answer key, or with a far stronger judge, chooses which new questions to answer no better than the untrained model does by sampling 32 answers and abstaining where they disagree; the grader's knowledge adds about one corrected answer per hundred questions. What a grader believes about a kind of question travels. A judge that rejects eleven of the twelve correct training answers about capitals of former states teaches the model to refuse 98% of such capitals on new questions, a loss that accuracy and abstention rates do not reveal. Changing only those twelve verdicts by hand moves the refusal from 5% to 90%, even for a grader that accepts as many answers as the answer key; at that leniency, two of four judges already cost 38-42% of these capitals. The capitals are not forgotten: with "I don't know" blocked, the model answers 94% of them correctly. The grader therefore needs no knowledge of its own: rewarding the model for giving the answer that most of its own untrained samples agree on, with no labels and no judge, earns the answer key's reward and keeps the category.

items.title: Researchers evaluate transfer effectiveness of post-hoc demographic framing mitigation policies on gender and age contrasts in climate messages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Objectives and Evaluators Disagree: Evaluating Transfer for Post-hoc Demographic Framing Mitigation
items.summary:
Researchers studied post-hoc rewriting methods to reduce demographic disparities in large language model-generated text when the original model is inaccessible. They analyzed 660 gender pairs and 1,980 age contrasts in demographic-conditioned climate messages, comparing fixed and adaptive editing policies using independent evaluators to assess framing disparity.

The study found that a fixed policy targeting messages with lower Persuasion Bias Index (PBI) transferred inconsistently, while an adaptive policy proposing edits on both sides but accepting at most one improved disparity reduction in most comparisons, though with higher preservation risk. Policies editing both messages achieved larger disparity reductions on fewer pairs. The results suggest that mitigation effectiveness varies across objectives, evaluators, prompts, and editing strategies, highlighting the need to report transfer outcomes comprehensively.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25258v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-hoc rewriting is used to reduce demographic disparities in LLM-generated text when the source model is inaccessible. A rewrite can look successful merely because it improved its own target or satisfied its selector. We study this as a transfer problem on 660 gender pairs and 1,980 age contrasts of demographic-conditioned climate messages. A rewriter proposes edits, a selection model chooses among constraint-satisfying candidates, and an independent evaluator uninvolved in either rates pairwise framing disparity. A fixed policy that always targets the message with the lower Persuasion Bias Index (PBI) transfers inconsistently across axes and outcome aggregations. An adaptive policy that proposes edits on both sides but accepts at most one significantly improves on that rule, applied to the same candidates, in seven of eight comparisons across two evaluator families, mostly by editing more pairs, not by guided direction choice, at higher preservation risk. A policy editing both messages gives the largest point reductions on fewer pairs. These two policies reduce disparity across a preservation-threshold sweep; absolute ratings vary across evaluator families and prompts. Shrinking the PBI gap increases dimension-mean disparity under both evaluator families. Mitigation should be reported as transfer across objectives, evaluators and their prompts, and editing policies.

items.title: Researchers evaluate confidence methods for zero-shot classification in 11 open-weight LLMs, finding logit-based scoring improves discrimination over black-box methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLMs Are Already Confidence-Aware Zero-Shot Classifiers
items.summary: Researchers compared black-box and white-box confidence estimation methods for zero-shot text classification using 11 open-weight large language models (1B-32B parameters) across five datasets with 3 to 151 labels. They found that while confidence method choice rarely affected accuracy, logit-based scoring methods significantly improved discrimination (AUROC 0.74-0.77) compared to black-box approaches (AUROC 0.57-0.66). The study also introduced decision-only scoring, which reduces decoding steps by 88-96% on large label sets with comparable performance to full-label scoring. The best open-weight model-method combinations, including Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.5 9B, performed competitively with a commercial classifier.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Zero-shot large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as text classifiers, but their labels are only useful when we know to what extent we can trust them. We compare black-box methods (verbalised confidence and sampling) with white-box methods that read token probabilities (P(True), and multiple logit-scoring methods using constrained generation). We evaluate eleven open-weight LLMs (1B-32B parameters) on five classification datasets with 3 to 151 labels, measuring classification performance (accuracy, F1-macro), discrimination (AUROC), and calibration (ECE and Brier score). The choice of confidence method rarely impacts accuracy significantly, but logit-based scoring methods lead to much better discrimination (AUROC 0.74-0.77) than black-box methods (AUROC 0.57-0.66). Replacing labels with single-token identifiers preserves discrimination but costs 3-6 accuracy points on average. We also introduce decision-only scoring, which only scores positions where labels diverge in the prefix tree (trie). It reduces decode steps by 88-96% on the three largest label sets and performs comparably to full-label scoring. The best open-weight model-method configurations (Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.5 9B) are competitive with the commercial Jev 1.13.0 classifier.

items.title: Researchers investigate continuous location representations to improve spatial generalization in large language models, evaluating on geo-text benchmarks for Los Angeles and London [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Geographic Memory to Spatial Generalization in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers distinguish geospatial memory from spatial generalization in large language models (LLMs), focusing on whether continuous location representations enhance the ability to predict geographic descriptions for unobserved locations. They introduce a latent spatial field concept, projecting continuous spatial encodings into the model's embedding space as spatial tokens, and evaluate this approach using new geo-text benchmarks for Los Angeles and London.

The study assesses geospatial captioning to test both memory and generalization, alongside a geospatial grounding model to evaluate the usefulness of generated location-description pairs for mapping text to geographic space. Results across multiple LLM families show that continuous location representations improve captioning at unobserved locations compared to textual coordinates and provide modest but consistent improvements in downstream grounding. Additional analysis supports the presence of spatially organized geographic representations within the models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can associate places with geographic descriptions, but recovering an observed association does not establish an ability to generalize across geographic space. We distinguish geospatial memory, the recovery of location--description associations observed during training, from spatial generalization, the prediction of descriptions for locations in unobserved regions. We investigate whether continuous location representations improve this generalization and encourage geographic knowledge to become spatially organized within an LLM. We frame this organization as a latent spatial field: a learned mapping from locations to descriptions connected through spatial dependencies. Building on a continuous spatial encoder, we project location representations into the model's embedding space and supply them as spatial tokens. We evaluate the resulting models on two newly curated geo-text benchmarks for Los Angeles and London using two complementary assessments. Layer-wise probing and representation clustering provide additional evidence consistent with spatially organized geographic representations. Together, these findings show the value of evaluating spatial generalization separately from memory and of incorporating continuous spatial representations into language models.

items.title: Researchers introduce CaRR framework to improve diffusion language model quality under low inference budgets using commitment-aware refinement and recovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Closing Performance Gap for Diffusion Language Models under Low Inference Budgets
items.summary: Researchers present CaRR, a training-free framework designed to enhance the output quality of diffusion language models at low inference budgets by employing updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within existing edit schedules. CaRR includes Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) and Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) modules that operate without additional backbone forwards to refine and recover candidate outputs. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning tasks demonstrate that CaRR consistently improves average accuracy over native editable diffusion language models, with the largest gains observed under tight inference budgets, including a 7.44 percentage point increase at one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models offer an architectural route to low-budget generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, which can reduce the number of sequential decoding steps relative to token-by-token autoregressive decoding. However, realizing this advantage at low budgets is challenging, as generation quality often declines when the number of denoising and refinement steps is reduced. Editable diffusion models address this quality loss through post-draft refinement, but useful intermediate results may still be lost before final submission. We introduce CaRR (Commitment-aware Refinement and Recovery), a training-free framework which improves submission quality from a fixed editable checkpoint through updated-context refill and trajectory-based recovery within its existing forward schedule. Token Commitment Remasking (TCR) remasks selected native pure replacements and refills them on the next scheduled edit forward using the updated context. Submission Commitment Recovery (SCR) uses the resulting refinement trajectory to recover supported candidates when the final response does not satisfy task-specific output requirements. Both modules operate within the native mask/edit schedule without additional backbone forwards. Experiments on code generation and mathematical reasoning show consistent gains in average accuracy over native ME-DLM across four inference budgets, with the largest gains under tight budgets. At one-eighth of the full scheduled forward budget, CaRR improves the six-metric average accuracy by 7.44 pp, including gains of 11.37 and 10.05 on MBPP and MBPP+.

items.title: Review examines clinical large language models' reasoning errors and proposes neuro-symbolic methods to verify logic and improve AI safety in medical applications [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Verifiable Logic in Medical LLMs: A Critical Review of Agentic Clinical Reasoning Optimization and Neuro-Symbolic Grounding
items.summary:
This review analyzes how clinical large language models (LLMs) can produce plausible but invalid reasoning that static benchmarks fail to detect, leading to hallucinations and flawed inferences. It covers four paradigms: the origins of clinical hallucination, the agentic hallucination cascade in multi-agent systems, process reward modeling for step-level supervision, and neuro-symbolic grounding that uses formal logic and knowledge graphs to constrain neural outputs. The authors argue that current evaluation and regulation focus on final answer accuracy without verifying reasoning steps, which poses safety risks in clinical AI.

The paper highlights that systems incorporating symbolic veto layers within their encoded domains can provide verifiable guarantees and improve safety metrics, though existing studies are limited to simulations or small samples and are not directly comparable to neural baselines. It proposes a conceptual framework linking agentic failure modes to symbolic intervention points and emphasizes that clinical AI safety depends heavily on system architecture. The authors advocate for certification processes that audit reasoning trajectories alongside static benchmark accuracy to ensure responsible deployment of medical AI.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical large language models are usually judged by whether the final answer is right. Yet a model can reach a fluent, plausible output through invalid reasoning that static benchmarks do not detect, and confident hallucination, causally invalid inference, and spurious demographic shortcuts can pass conventional evaluation. This critical review covers four paradigms in turn: how clinical hallucination arises and why static metrics miss it; the agentic hallucination cascade, in which multi-agent and tool-augmented systems propagate and amplify early reasoning errors; process reward modeling as step-level supervision; and neuro-symbolic grounding, in which formal logic engines, ontology reasoners, and knowledge graphs place verifiable constraints on neural output. Within their encoded domains, systems with symbolic veto layers offer guarantees that hold relative to their encoded knowledge, and they report large gains on the safety measures they use. These results come from single studies, mostly in simulated or small-sample settings, and are not directly comparable with neural baselines. Process reward models remain bounded by the statistics of their training data. We propose a conceptual framework that maps each agentic failure mode to a symbolic intervention point, and we argue that clinical AI safety depends substantially on system architecture. Because current regulation emphasizes performance and does not require verification of reasoning steps, we argue that responsible certification should also audit reasoning trajectories alongside accuracy on static benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers propose PoolDPP, a determinantal point process-based method to improve diversity in language model sampling with theoretical guarantees and empirical gains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Model of Diverse Sampling from Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers introduce PoolDPP, a method that models diverse generation from language models as sampling subsets from a determinantal point process (DPP), balancing item quality and diversity by repelling similar outputs. Since exact inference is intractable, PoolDPP draws a candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weights candidates, and applies a $K$-DPP sampler or a greedy MAP variant for deterministic selection, with a proven finite-sample bound on approximation quality.

Empirical results show PoolDPP extends the quality-diversity frontier in open-ended text generation and improves precision-recall trade-offs in ambiguous text-to-SQL tasks and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, increasing diversity without sacrificing accuracy at comparable sample sizes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models often produce high-quality individual samples but poor sets, with repeated samples clustering around the same semantic modes. We formalize diverse generation as sampling a size-$K$ subset of complete strings from a determinantal point process (DPP), where the likelihood encodes item quality, and the embedding geometry encodes repulsion between similar outputs. Exact inference over all strings is intractable, so we propose PoolDPP: draw a finite candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weight the candidates toward the target quality, and run a $K$-DPP sampler on the induced pool kernel; a greedy MAP variant provides deterministic selection. We prove a finite-sample bound with an explicit constant: the KL divergence between the sampler's output and the target $K$-DPP decays as O(1/N) in the pool size. Empirically, PoolDPP extends the quality--diversity frontier on open-ended generation and the precision--recall frontier on ambiguous text-to-SQL (Ambrosia), and on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), it raises diversity at about the same pass@$K$.

items.title: Researchers introduce InflEns, a game-theoretic mixture of LoRA experts for data allocation that predicts expert specialization and routing without training explicit gates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Game-Theoretic Data Allocation for Expert Specialization and Routing
items.summary: Researchers present InflEns, a framework that uses a location game in a fixed prompt-trait space to allocate training data and inference routing among LoRA experts, enabling prediction of which expert will perform best on a given prompt. Evaluated on seven safety-related benchmarks, InflEns shows that the expert with the highest share of prompts achieves the lowest negative log-likelihood on about 90% of cases, outperforming random allocations and matching learned gating methods without explicit gate training. The fixed routing allows identification and retraining of harmful experts, significantly reducing attack success while maintaining instruction following. InflEns offers control over expert specialization through kernel choice, trait-space geometry, and expert count, and can be extended to various encoders and data distributions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can the allocation used to train experts also predict which expert will perform best on a prompt? Such a connection would make the intended division of labor inspectable before training and allow the allocation itself to guide inference. We introduce InflEns, a mixture of LoRA experts whose training weights and inference routes come from the same location game in a fixed prompt-trait space. Players choose positions to maximize their expected shares of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses. We utilize the game's kernel-general theoretical criterion for when co-located positions become locally unstable to separation. We evaluate InflEns on a corpus assembled from seven safety-related benchmarks, which demonstrates that the highest-share expert has the lowest held-out response negative log-likelihood (NLL) on approximately 90% of prompts across four kernels under a sharpened simplex representation, compared with approximately 15% after permuting allocations across prompts. We demonstrate that the method performs comparably to published learned gates without having to train an explicit gate on the experts. Because the router is fixed, we can trace harmful behavior to a single expert and retrain only that expert, which lowers HarmBench attack success from 0.51 to 0.02 while keeping instruction following. The game also gives us several controls over how the experts specialize, including the kernel choice and its parameters, the trait-space geometry, and the number of experts. Importantly, InflEns is a general framework that can be extended to any encoder and data distribution.

items.title: Researchers introduce PosteriorBench to evaluate algorithms for efficient behavior posterior sampling in language models using 21 tasks on Qwen3.5-0.8B [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PosteriorBench: Evaluating Behavior Posterior Sampling in Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers present PosteriorBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate algorithms that sample from a language model's distribution over transcripts exhibiting rare behaviors. The benchmark includes 21 tasks on the Qwen3.5-0.8B model with behavior probabilities ranging from 10^-5 to 10^-1, using exact posterior samples from a corpus of one billion labeled responses to measure compute cost and sample fidelity via KL divergence.

The study finds that existing methods either lack efficiency or faithfulness: simple prompting methods are computationally cheap but yield high divergence from the true posterior, fine-tuning on posterior samples is often too costly, and prior training methods do not improve performance. The researchers highlight that developing a cost-effective posterior sampler remains an open challenge and provide code and data to facilitate progress in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25735v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rare language model behaviors can be difficult to study because obtaining them through ordinary sampling can require a very large number of samples. This motivates the behavior posterior sampling problem: given a language model and a behavior of interest, is there an algorithm that efficiently samples from the model's distribution over transcripts that exhibit this behavior? We introduce PosteriorBench, a benchmark for comparing algorithms by their compute cost and by how close their samples are to the true posterior in forward and reverse KL divergence. PosteriorBench contains 21 tasks on Qwen3.5-0.8B with behavior probabilities from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-1}$, each with exact posterior samples from a corpus of one billion labeled responses. We find that no method we evaluate is both efficient and faithful: simple methods like prompting are cheap but plateau at a high KL divergence from the posterior, fine-tuning on posterior samples is often cost-prohibitive, and several training methods from prior work do not perform better. Building a posterior sampler that can cheaply approximate the true posterior remains an open problem, and we hope PosteriorBench can measure progress towards this objective. Code and data are available at https://github.com/TransluceAI/PosteriorBench.

items.originalTitle: Anchor and Check: Deterministic Cross-Prompt, Cross-Model Reconciliation for Auditable LLM Decisions
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a reconciliation contract for large language models (LLMs) that commits to a target model's greedy answer (the anchor) and verifies it with one or two checks from alternate prompts or different model families. This method returns one of five outcomes, acting only on agreement, to ensure decisions are auditable and reproducible despite generation variability on hosted APIs. The approach was evaluated on 48,000 model-item pairs across 6,000 questions, showing that pooling samples from different model families improves semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points compared to same-model temperature checks, which performed weakest.

The contract automates decisions on 70% of items while still acting on 16% of errors, outperforming pooled entropy detectors with fewer samples under various tie-breaker conventions. It provides a fixed committed answer, explicit outcomes, and replayable decision records, addressing reproducibility challenges in LLM pipelines that make discrete decisions unattended.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pipelines that let a large language model (LLM) make discrete decisions need to know which decisions they may act on unattended, and a record that explains each one. We study a small, fully specified reconciliation contract: commit the target model's greedy answer (the anchor), draw one or two greedy checks that reach the answer by a different route (an alternate prompt, or a model from another family), and let a pure function return one of five outcomes, of which only Agree is acted on. On 48,000 model-item evaluations over 6,000 questions, with every method given access to verbalized confidence as a tie-breaker, the main finding concerns where calls come from: pooling another family's samples raises semantic entropy's AUROC by 1.7 to 4.0 points at every budget, and a same-model temperature check is the weakest design. As complete pipelines, the point estimates of the three-call contract and pooled semantic entropy over 3 or 5 samples differ by less than one point, with intervals containing zero. As detectors of the anchor's errors, the contract is ahead of pooled entropy with 3 and 5 samples under both tie-breaker conventions; with 10 samples the point estimates differ by less than one point and the sign depends on the convention. Under the strict Agree gate it automates 70% of items and still acts on 16% of errors. What the contract adds is a fixed committed answer, an explicit outcome and a decision replayable from its record; generation itself was not reproducible on the hosted API.

items.title: Researchers propose Task-Calibrated Denoising Allocation to adapt inference schedules for diffusion language models, certifying cost reductions across tasks and models with error guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: One Schedule Does Not Fit All: Adaptive Inference Schedules for Diffusion Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Task-Calibrated Denoising Allocation (TCDA), a method that adapts denoising schedules in diffusion language models based on task, model, and sampler characteristics to reduce computational cost while preserving output quality. TCDA uses calibration data and statistical bounds to certify the cheapest feasible inference schedule or revert to the full schedule, maintaining an asymptotic error probability below a set threshold.

The approach was tested on seven datasets and two model families, achieving denoiser evaluation reductions ranging from 1.33 to 8 times depending on the task and model. Validation on fresh data confirmed the reliability of schedule selections, with false certification rates below 2%. The study also found that schedule effectiveness varies with task and model scale, and that reproducible comparisons require fixing the random time grid used by the ELF reference sampler.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.25895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models typically use a fixed denoising schedule across workloads. We show that the cheapest schedule that preserves quality depends on the task, model, and sampler. We propose Task-Calibrated Denoising Allocation (TCDA), a deployment rule with an explicit error guarantee. Given candidate samplers, paired calibration data, a utility tolerance, and guardrails against degeneration, TCDA uses simultaneous one-sided bootstrap bounds to certify which candidates meet both the utility and guardrail criteria. It deploys the cheapest certified candidate or falls back to the full schedule. The probability of deploying an infeasible schedule is asymptotically at most alpha. Candidates include early prefix decoding, state-reusing continuation, reduced time grids, and confidence-threshold decoding. Across seven datasets and two model families, TCDA certifies reductions in denoiser evaluations by factors of 3.4 on XSum and 2.0 on WMT14 for ELF-B; 8.0 on WMT14 and 4.1 on GSM8K for LLaDA-8B; and 1.33 on OpenWebText for both ELF-M and ELF-L. A validation protocol fixed before generation confirmed every selection on fresh seeds. Across 500 calibration splits, false certification remained below 2% in every setting at a nominal level of 5%. Certified schedules vary across tasks and model scales. Trajectory measurements suggest that when decoded tokens commit is more informative for schedule selection than the remaining latent discretization error. We also find that the ELF reference sampler draws its time grid at random, so reproducible schedule comparisons for unconditional generation require fixing the grid.

items.title: Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Policy Improvement-Guided Replay for Continual Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.25989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires models to acquire new capabilities while retaining performance on previous tasks. A stability-oriented perspective common in conventional continual learning emphasizes knowledge preservation and interference mitigation. Complementing this perspective, we revisit CRL for vision-language models through policy improvement, a fundamental principle of RL, to preserve acquired performance gains. Using the performance difference lemma, we characterize historical performance changes through the current policy's expected advantages on historical task distributions, motivating replay of historical prompts with the current policy. To allocate limited replay memory, we propose Contrastive Likelihood Replay (CoLiR), which contrasts likelihood gains on correct responses from the final task policy with likelihood reductions on incorrect responses from the initial policy. Our analysis links correct-response likelihood gains to reference-policy advantages under an idealized KL-regularized optimal update and provides an endogenous-reward interpretation for general policy updates. CoLiR estimates scores from finite training rollouts and cached log-likelihoods, selects prompts at task boundaries, and replays them uniformly during subsequent training, with KL regularization restricted to replayed prompts. Memory construction only requires a small amount of additional cross-policy scoring but no additional response generation. Across three Qwen3-VL model sizes on MRCL, CoLiR achieves the highest mean final accuracy and mean task accuracy among the compared methods while maintaining competitive new-task performance.

items.title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.26248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.

items.title: PhoneWorld: From Real-App Trajectories to Dynamic and Verifiable Environments for Phone-Use Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PhoneWorld: From Real-App Trajectories to Dynamic and Verifiable Environments for Phone-Use Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2605.29486v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Real applications provide the training setting closest to phone-agent deployment, but are difficult to reset, scale safely, and verify programmatically. Static screenshots and interaction trajectories preserve realistic evidence but cannot generate new experience. We introduce PhoneWorld, a trace-grounded framework that converts such evidence into runnable, resettable, and verifiable Android environments. PhoneWorld induces a usage-weighted interaction skeleton from observed pages, transitions, and state-changing operations; translates it into a behavior-grounded app specification; realizes the specification through an autonomous build--inspect--repair loop; and synthesizes executable tasks with programmatic verifiers. The resulting suite spans 34 consumer-facing apps across 16 domains and supports an audited online benchmark, verified trajectory generation, and online RL through common reset and verification interfaces. Evaluations with diverse general and open-source GUI agents show that PhoneWorld supports reliable end-to-end online interaction and exposes capabilities complementary to AndroidWorld. Controlled SFT experiments further show that PhoneWorld trajectories complement AndroidWorld supervision, transfer across online and offline benchmarks, and become more effective as data volume and app coverage increase. Under a matched RL budget, combining PhoneWorld mock-app rollouts with real-app rollouts improves performance over real-app RL alone on both real-phone tasks and AndroidWorld. Together, these results demonstrate that trace-grounded executable abstraction can bridge realistic mobile behavior and scalable agent learning, turning limited real-app evidence into a growing supply of controllable and verifiable environments for training and evaluation.

items.title: Supportive Token Revealing for Fast Diffusion Language Model Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Supportive Token Revealing for Fast Diffusion Language Model Decoding
items.summary: arXiv:2606.04236v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Discrete diffusion language models can generate text efficiently by updating multiple masked positions in parallel, but this parallelism introduces a quality-latency trade-off. Aggressive decoding may commit mutually dependent tokens too early, while conservative decoding requires many denoising steps. Existing methods address this tension by deciding which tokens are safe to reveal using confidence or dependency criteria. However, avoiding unsafe commits does not necessarily make the remaining masked sequence easy to decode, since uncertain tokens may depend on masked tokens, creating a bottleneck for denoising steps. We propose AXON, a training-free module that can be added on top of existing parallel decoding strategies for diffusion language models. Rather than replacing the base decoder, AXON monitors the remaining uncertain masked tokens and intervenes only when their current state suggests that additional context is needed. It then shifts the criterion from which tokens are safest to reveal to which confident reveals would best support later denoising. AXON selects anchors, confident masked tokens that uncertain positions attend to, using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals. Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks across multiple diffusion language models show that AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off of existing parallel decoders, often reducing the number of function evaluations while maintaining or improving accuracy.

Aggressive decoding may commit mutually dependent tokens too early, while conservative decoding requires many denoising steps. Existing methods address this tension by deciding which tokens are safe to reveal using confidence or dependency criteria. However, avoiding unsafe commits does not necessarily make the remaining masked sequence easy to decode, since uncertain tokens may depend on masked tokens, creating a bottleneck for denoising steps. We propose AXON, a training-free module that can be added on top of existing parallel decoding strategies for diffusion language models. Rather than replacing the base decoder, AXON monitors the remaining uncertain masked tokens and intervenes only when their current state suggests that additional context is needed. It then shifts the criterion from which tokens are safest to reveal to which confident reveals would best support later denoising. AXON selects anchors, confident masked tokens that uncertain positions attend to, using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals. Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks across multiple diffusion language models show that AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off of existing parallel decoders, often reducing the number of function evaluations while maintaining or improving accuracy.

items.title: STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: STEPQuant: When and Where Errors Matter in Delta-Rule Recurrent State Quantization
items.summary: arXiv:2609.38169v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Linear attention replaces growing KV caches with fixed-size recurrent states, yet these persistent states can become a substantial memory bottleneck under concurrent serving. Directly quantizing recurrent states to low precision often leads to severe accuracy degradation, as quantization errors propagate through successive state updates. We discover that the impact of these errors depends on two complementary dimensions: temporally, errors in long-lived memory can persist across many decoding steps; spatially, errors in different key rows affect model outputs differently, while state magnitudes vary substantially along both rows and columns. Motivated by these observations, we propose STEPQuant, a spatial-temporal post-training quantization framework for Delta-rule recurrent states. STEPQuant allocates precision according to error magnitude and memory lifetime, and jointly fits key-row and value-column scales based on state distributions and key-row impact on output error. Experiments on Qwen3.8-27B and Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct across both long- and short-generation benchmarks show that STEPQuant closely matches FP32-state accuracy under a nominal 6-bit budget and outperforms uniform INT8 in its 4-bit configuration. Integrated into SGLang with optimized GPU kernels, 6-bit STEPQuant achieves over 5x recurrent-state compression and reduces total serving memory by up to 68.7%. Our code is available at https://github.com/Dreamer-Toby/STEPQuant.

items.title: Capturing In-Context Learning Dynamics with Task Operators [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Capturing In-Context Learning Dynamics with Task Operators
items.summary: arXiv:2610.01054v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to perform new tasks from demonstrations without weight updates. However, every ICL inference requires processing the full set of examples, resulting in inefficient deployments, and how ICL works mechanistically is not fully understood. Prior work compresses ICL into fixed activation vectors extracted from specific layers or positions, but these input-independent interventions fail on complex tasks where the output depends on fine-grained interactions with the input. By analyzing the ICL forward pass, we show that each attention head's output is an affine transformation of its context-masked counterpart, and that the parameters of this transformation are empirically stable across samples for a given task. Building on this, we introduce Task Operator (TO), which replays this transformation as an analytically derived update to the attention output projection. Across lexical, algorithmic, and reasoning tasks, TO achieves the best overall performance among prior methods and substantially narrows the gap between zero-shot inference and ICL. We further show that the extracted knowledge concentrates in a task-specific sparse circuit across layers and positions, and that averaging operators from disjoint demonstration batches enables effective many-shot scaling without expanding the context window. Our code is available at https://github.com/gzxiong/task_operator.

items.title: AVSD: Adaptive-View Self-Distillation by Balancing Consensus and Teacher-Specific Privileged Signals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AVSD: Adaptive-View Self-Distillation by Balancing Consensus and Teacher-Specific Privileged Signals
items.summary: arXiv:2605.20643v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-distillation enables language models to learn on-policy from their own trajectories by using the same model as both student and teacher, with the teacher being conditioned on privileged information unavailable to the student. Such information can come in different types or views, such as solutions, demonstrations, feedback, or final answers. This setup provides dense token-level feedback without relying on a separate external model, but creates a fundamental asymmetry: the teacher may rely on view-specific information that the student cannot access at inference time. Moreover, the best type of privileged information is often task-dependent, making it difficult to choose a single teacher view. In this work, we address both these challenges jointly by introducing AVSD (Adaptive-View Self-Distillation), a novel method of self-distillation with multiple privileged-information views, which reconstructs token-level supervision by separating stable cross-view consensus from view-specific residual signals. AVSD identifies the consensus signal shared across views, which provides a reliable update direction, and then selectively adds the view-specific residual signal to adjust the update magnitude when it both aligns with the consensus direction and remains proportionate to the consensus signal. Experiments on math competition benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25) show that AVSD consistently outperforms both single-view self-distillation baselines and GRPO, achieving average Avg@8 gains of 3.1% and 2.2% over the strongest baselines on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B, respectively. Moreover, on code-generation benchmarks (Codeforces, LiveCodeBench v6) using Qwen3-8B, AVSD outperforms the single-view self-distillation baseline by 2.4% on average.

items.title: VESTA: Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: VESTA: Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2606.00384v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fitting quantitative models to data is a central step in scientific workflows, yet it remains one of the least automated. Recent agent-based systems leverage language and vision-language models (VLMs) to propose statistical models, but these systems struggle on challenging modeling tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce VESTA (Visual Exploration with Statistical Tool Agents), a framework that equips VLMs with a dynamically growing toolkit to guide model refinement through data transformations, hypothesis-driven visualizations, and statistical tests. Unlike prior systems that rely on iterative critique alone, VESTA explores data before and during refinement by selecting or creating reusable diagnostic tools. We evaluate VESTA using three toolkit configurations: no tools, static expert-written tools, and dynamic model-written tools. To support this evaluation, we introduce DAWN (Dataset for Automated Workflows and Numerical Modeling), a benchmark targeting distribution fitting and time series modeling with varying difficulty tiers that culminates in real-world astronomy tasks including modeling initial mass functions and gravitational-wave chirp signals. VESTA's dynamic tool creation outperforms prior agentic pipelines for statistical analysis and visual tool creation, with the largest gains on complex and domain-specific tasks. Against strong agentic coding harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode), VESTA is better on all time series tasks and on complex distribution fitting tasks, though the harnesses achieve better fits on simpler distributions. Further, dynamically generated tools are substantially more sophisticated than those produced by existing visual tool-creation systems, covering more diagnostic categories per function and strongly preferring visual outputs that the VESTA VLM critic can reason over directly.

items.title: Balance of Benchmarks: Evidence Retention and Multiplicity-Aware Model Comparison [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Balance of Benchmarks: Evidence Retention and Multiplicity-Aware Model Comparison
items.summary: arXiv:2608.30044v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Benchmark aggregation requires decisions about how much evidence to use and how much influence each benchmark receives. Curated suites control influence through selection, which can exclude informative observations. A broader pool can retain those observations. With equal weighting, repeated or closely related benchmarks gain influence as their number grows. We introduce Balance of Benchmarks (BoB) to retain eligible observations and control their influence separately. We fit benchmark-specific response curves to place different difficulty ranges on a shared ability scale and use description similarity to downweight benchmarks in crowded neighborhoods. We test retention and density weighting in separate interventions on WildScores, a sparse collection of 148 developer-reported benchmarks, using 14 Artificial Analysis benchmarks as a controlled reference. With the model population fixed and entire source-lineage families held out, suite expansion improves held-out prediction under BoB and equal-weight equating on both WildScores and BIG-bench. Under substantial reporting overlap, density weighting improves robustness to multiplicity. Complete re-listings yield smaller mean rank displacement under BoB (0.63 versus 1.95 for equal-weight equating), with benefits also in paraphrased re-listings and supported affine fits. The benefit can reverse if models report different benchmarks, because a single weight per column gives models that report only part of a group less than its intended share. We therefore compute each model's weights from the benchmarks it reports. This rule removes the reversal in controlled re-listings and keeps held-out prediction close to that of equal weighting. These comparisons separate evidence retention, benchmark influence, and reporting coverage and show why repeated entries need to be handled per model.

items.title: Clause-Factored Bilateral State Grounding and Scoped Passivity for Counterfactual Open-World Deductive Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Clause-Factored Bilateral State Grounding and Scoped Passivity for Counterfactual Open-World Deductive Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2609.37351v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Open-World Assumption (OWA) deduction requires distinguishing provable facts (True), refutations (False), and unprovable statements (Unknown) across counterfactual edits and unseen domains. Sequence and latent-recurrent transformers rely on distributional shortcuts, whereas chain-of-thought language models incur high autoregressive latency. We decompose OWA deduction into a clause-factored bilateral grounder ($F$) and a deductive deliberation operator ($B$), forming $B \circ F$ in Typed Edge-Factorized Bilateral Port-Hamiltonian Deliberation (TE-BPHD). Trained solely on three-way query labels without parsers or proof-depth annotations, TE-BPHD (37.85M parameters) maps clauses into a 1,440-dimensional Belnap space and propagates support through passivity-balanced implicit Port-Hamiltonian rule diodes. Across 17,036 locked ProofWriter test queries, TE-BPHD reaches 79.17 +/- 5.48% depth-5 counterfactual consistency (+23.83 to +38.67 percentage points over Seq2Seq T5, Flan-T5, and Recurrent-Depth T5) and 94.95 +/- 1.23% out-of-distribution (OOD) accuracy across 5,270 six-domain queries (92.54 +/- 3.38% macro-mean). On a paired 120-query OOD slice, TE-BPHD attains 93.61 +/- 4.59% versus 79.17% for 3-shot Qwen3-1.7B under a 2,048-token reasoning cap (+14.44 percentage points) at 9.44 versus 14,878.4 ms/query batch-16 NVIDIA L4 throughput. Operator interventions show that symmetric single-rule passivity prevents positive two-cycle modes seen in Gain-Matched Unilateral Horn (+50.00 percentage points counterfactual consistency), whereas unit-interval Grounded Product-T-Norm Logic Tensor Networks (LTN) achieve cycle-safe OOD transfer (94.50 +/- 0.87%) without linear solves, and multi-fact ParaRules prose exposes an upstream grounding trade-off (1.33 +/- 1.76% zero-shot vs. 34.11 +/- 5.01% with five-slot optimal-transport joint grounding).

items.title: Can Computation from Earlier Problems Help LLMs Solve New Ones? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Computation from Earlier Problems Help LLMs Solve New Ones?
items.summary: arXiv:2609.39394v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models often solve independent problems in the same conversation. Can computation from earlier problems help them solve new ones? Preliminary experiments show that retained history can raise or lower later-turn accuracy, even within the same domain. To trace this effect, we hold each problem fixed and vary its preceding history. The resulting changes in the model's internal states contain a recurring, problem-dependent component. To improve reasoning with retained history, we introduce STAIR (Stale-Token Attention for Inter-query Reuse). It captures attention keys and values from earlier response generation in a read-only bank. STAIR learns to reflect current query vectors to redirect attention over this bank during prompt processing. The backbone and stored entries remain fixed; only 12,288 parameters are trained. Across three Qwen models and four reasoning benchmarks, STAIR improves average later-turn accuracy by up to 11.67 percentage points over the unmodified model with history. The math-trained Qwen3.5-9B controller also improves code generation on HumanEval+ without further training.

items.title: REACT: Representational Early Analysis and Control of Chain-of-Thought Trajectories [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: REACT: Representational Early Analysis and Control of Chain-of-Thought Trajectories
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32113v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) generation offers an opportunity to intervene before a reasoning model completes its answer. How does the safety effect of a single activation edit vary across early reasoning states, and what factors govern that variation? We study this question with REACT, a conditional activation intervention that learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories and applies it once to an early CoT hidden state. The model weights remain frozen, and all subsequent tokens are generated without further edits. To study timing, we train directions separately at each of the first five CoT positions and evaluate ungated edits with full post-edit regeneration. Across three DeepSeek-R1 distilled models, site-specific edits concentrate safety gains in the opening CoT tokens. Norm-matched controls on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (8B) disentangle two factors behind this curve: holding an effective direction and edit budget fixed still yields much larger early ($t_1$-$t_5$) than later ($t_6$-$t_8$) gains, whereas the near-zero site-specific $t_3$ gain reflects higher optimisation variance despite rising risk-probe AUROC. Forced prefixes shift the high-gain region with the opening context, and a four-arm intervention shows that ~98% of the net gain at $t_2$ propagates through the changed next token. On the same 8B model, REACT raises the rate of fully safe CoT-answer outputs on StrongREJECT-273 from 29.06% to 82.05%, while keeping benign refusal and usefulness near baseline. An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/REACT_official2-333B.

items.title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking
items.summary: arXiv:2611.18639v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both interactive worlds and the tasks agents must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation (WD). World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. Explicit states and tool-call traces support task validation and agent evaluation. We evaluate 22 models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 88.8% mean Pass@1. Construction experiments demonstrate token efficiency and expansion of task coverage. At the richest knowledge level, WD fully covers 22/23 properties, 19/29 functionalities, and 30/39 event requirements specified in a real RobotVacuum protocol. Furthermore, the 1,000 sampled tasks semantically cover 81.6% of the 854 reference instructions in the real-world corpus. SynthDCB connects an expanding space of real-to-sim executable capabilities to verifiable agent evaluation.

items.title: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation
items.summary: arXiv:2611.24254v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.
items.description: arXiv:2611.24254v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. items.title: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules
items.summary: arXiv:2611.24869v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

items.title: Weight Space Programming for Vision Language Model Repair
items.originalTitle: Weight Space Programming for Vision Language Model Repair
items.summary: arXiv:2611.23615v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In weight-space programming, a language model edits a network's weights directly, without gradients. We ask what a successful repair of this kind relies on. We plant faults in the weights of two vision-language models, SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M, and check each edit made by a coding agent against the original weights. Without being told where to look, the agent finds rescaled projector rows and noise in the vision encoder, infers the unknown scale factors, and returns most or all of the rescaled weights to their exact original values and accuracy to near its original level. These repairs depend on a trace of how the faults were computed. The original weights have 16-bit precision, and faults computed in 32-bit arithmetic leave low bits that only the damaged weights carry, a cue that a real failure need not leave. When we round those bits away, each model answers our test questions as before, but the agent, unaided, no longer repairs either model: on LFM2-VL accuracy recovers by about 4 points, against 17 from the unrounded weights. Marking the damaged weights again in their low bits brings the edits back to them. Rounded weights still hold statistical evidence of the rescaling. On SmolVLM the agent uses it once a sentence in the prompt, which we wrote knowing the fault, names such a statistic; on LFM2-VL, whose scale factors are larger, most sessions find the rescaled rows unaided, but none finds the noise. Swapped rows or columns, which keep the set of stored values, are not found unaided on either model within our budgets. We recommend that studies of weight repair report the number format of the weights and include a rounded control.
